verses.translation_literal: A prayer of David. Hear, YHWH, righteousness; give heed to my cry; give ear [to] my prayer, [which is] not from lips of deceit.
verses.translation_dramatic: A prayer of David. Hear me, LORD. Hear what is just. Listen to my cry as it rises, bend your ear to my prayer: it comes from no lying lips, only from one whose mouth and heart are one.
verses.directors_commentary:
The speaker opens with three commands in a row: 'hear', 'give heed', 'give ear'. Nothing is polite about it. This is the voice of someone in the legal dock who demands a hearing before a king, and in the ancient Near East a petitioner could often do no more than cry out at the gate. The word 'cry' (rinnah) is loud, a shout or a keening that carries across a distance; the commentators say it can be joy or entreaty, and here it is plainly entreaty (Radak on Psalm 17:1).

The KJV 'Hear the right, O Lord' softens the opening. The Hebrew has no 'the': it says 'hear, YHWH, righteousness', and the word tzedek can be the thing heard (a just cause), the manner of the hearing, or the kind of prayer (Ibn Ezra, Radak). The KJV also turns the last clause into a relative ('that goeth not out of feigned lips') where Hebrew simply says 'not lips of deceit'. The claim is stark: my words and my heart agree. The superscription is the first clause of the verse in the Hebrew, not a separate heading as the KJV prints it. Some medieval readers hear a repentant David here after Bathsheba (Meiri on Psalm 17:1), and others a hunted David; the text itself names no enemy yet.

philological_notes.note: Righteousness, justice, a just cause. The commentators divide on whether it is the object of 'hear' or describes the prayer; it is left bare, and the reader hears both.
My cry. The root rnn covers a ringing cry of joy as well as a shout of distress; here a loud petition.
Lips of deceit, an idiom for lying speech. 'Lips' stands for the speaker's words as a public act.

verses.translation_literal: From before you my judgment will go out; your eyes will see uprightness.
verses.translation_dramatic: Let my verdict come from your own face, and no other. Your eyes see what is level and true, and they will see it in me.
verses.directors_commentary:
Here the petitioner places the case before the highest court. 'From before you' means from your presence, from the throne itself; he asks that his verdict be issued there, and not by human judges. The idiom matters: in the ancient world a ruler's sentence went out from his face, and a sentence from the face of the God who sees truth is the one thing a falsely accused man could trust.

The KJV 'Let my sentence come forth from thy presence; let thine eyes behold the things that are equal' turns two statements into wishes. The Hebrew verbs are imperfects and can be wishes or confident futures; the ASV and KJV go for wishes, the YLT for plain statements. 'Equal' is Elizabethan for 'level, even': meisharim is the straight, flat road, the opposite of crooked. The medieval commentators divide sharply on what is happening. Rashi hears a man who knows he has sins and asks that his penalty not reach the throne; Malbim hears a man who knows human judges will convict him and asks that God's court decide instead (Rashi, Malbim on Psalm 17:2). The Hebrew allows both.

philological_notes.note: Levelness, uprightness, straightness; used of a smooth road and of fair judgment. KJV 'things that are equal' means 'level things'.

verses.translation_literal: You have tested my heart, you have visited [me by] night, you have smelted me; you will find [nothing]: I have resolved, my mouth shall not transgress.
verses.translation_dramatic: You have tested my heart. You have come to me in the night. You have set me in the fire like silver, and you will find no dross in me. I made up my mind: let my mouth never go beyond what is true.
verses.directors_commentary:
Three verbs in the perfect, one after another, and each is more intimate than the last: you have tested, you have visited, you have smelted. 'Tested' is the word for assaying a metal; 'smelted' (tzaraf) is the refiner's own verb, melting ore until the impurity floats out. The speaker says: put me through the fire; you will find nothing left to blame. 'Visited' (paqad) is the word for a divine inspection and also for the care a god pays his own; Metzudat Zion links it to 'the LORD visited Sarah' (Metzudat Zion on Psalm 17:3). The night is when a man is alone with his thoughts (Ibn Ezra, Metzudat David).

The KJV 'shalt find nothing' adds 'nothing' as an object that the Hebrew does not have: it says only 'you will not find'. Rashi supplies 'your desire'; Radak 'that I was unclean'. The last clause is hard. KJV 'I am purposed that my mouth shall not transgress' follows the verb zamam, 'to plan'; the YLT 'My thoughts pass not over my mouth' takes zimmah as a noun, meaning thought and speech do not part. Either way the point is the same as verse 1: nothing in the mind that the mouth would not say. Rashi hears Bathsheba here (the evening in 2 Samuel 11:2); Meiri reads it as a general statement (Rashi, Meiri on Psalm 17:3).

philological_notes.note: To smelt, refine. The verb of the goldsmith who melts down metal to burn off impurity. Stronger than the neutral 'tried' of the KJV.
You have visited, inspected, taken account of. Covers both a ruler's inspection and a god's gracious care.
I have resolved, planned; or, taken as a noun, 'my plan'. Disputed; the old versions differ.

verses.translation_literal: As for the deeds of humankind, by the word of your lips I [myself] have kept the paths of the violent one.
verses.translation_dramatic: As for what men do, I have watched. By the word of your own lips I kept away from the roads the violent walk.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is the hardest verse of the opening, and the translators split. The Hebrew has no 'from': it says 'I have kept (shamarti) the paths of the violent one'. Rashi reads it as 'I have watched them in order to turn aside from them'; Ibn Ezra and Radak as 'I have set guards on the paths of the violent so that no one will cross what your lips have said', so David protects others as well; Metzudat David as 'I have kept them closed so that no one may walk there' (Rashi, Ibn Ezra, Radak, Metzudat David on Psalm 17:4). The KJV 'I have kept me from the paths of the destroyer' follows the first reading and supplies 'me from'.

The word pariz is not 'destroyer' (KJV) but 'the violent one', literally 'the one who breaks through', the man who tears down fences and takes by force. It echoes the image of the breached wall. 'The word of your lips' is the divine command: Rashi quotes 'You shall not commit adultery' (Exodus 20:13), which is why he relates the verse to Bathsheba. 'The deeds of humankind' is bluntly general: 'adam' is the human race, not an individual.

philological_notes.note: One who breaks through: a robber, a violent man. From the root for breaching a wall. KJV 'destroyer' is too vague.
Paths, courses, ways of life. Often the figure for a way of living, as here.

verses.translation_literal: Holding firm [are] my steps in your tracks; my footsteps have not been shaken.
verses.translation_dramatic: My steps hold firm in your tracks. My feet have not slipped.
verses.directors_commentary:
The verse starts with an infinitive, 'to hold firm', with no stated subject or tense, and the readers split. The KJV and Webster take it as a prayer ('Hold up my goings'), the ASV and BBE as a report ('My steps have held fast'), and the YLT as an aim. Radak reads the infinitive as standing in the place of a command, as in 'Keep the sabbath day' (Deut 5:12) and 'Go and cry' (Jer 2:2); Meiri reads it as standing in the place of the past, 'I have held my steps in your tracks'. Meiri's reading fits the second clause, 'my footsteps have not been shaken', which is a perfect.

The KJV 'goings' and 'paths' are not wrong but dated. The word ma'gal is a track or circuit; Malbim reads it as the winding way that sometimes bends from the straight path to reach it (Malbim on Psalm 17:5), and Metzudat David simply glosses it 'paths'. 'Footsteps' (pe'amim) can also mean 'feet', as Metzudat Zion says. This is a man who describes his walk as steady in a world where a slipping foot is the standard image for falling to enemies or to sin.

philological_notes.note: Infinitive: 'holding firm', 'to hold fast'. It has no subject or tense of its own. Radak takes it as a command ('uphold'), Meiri as a past ('I have held'); English must choose, and the literal layer keeps the bare participle-like 'holding firm'.
Your tracks, courses, circuits. The path as a worn course.

verses.translation_literal: I, I have called you, for you will answer me, O God; incline your ear to me, hear my utterance.
verses.translation_dramatic: I call on you, God, because you answer. Turn your ear to me. Listen to what I say.
verses.directors_commentary:
The turn of the psalm. After the defense comes the request, and it begins with a stressed pronoun: 'I, I have called you.' The Hebrew has 'I' standing alone at the head of the line, which the KJV drops. It sets this caller against the 'they' who surround him in the next verses. The reason is given at once: 'for you will answer me'. The verb is an imperfect, and on the plain reading the confidence rests on a pattern, not on a guess; Rashi, Meiri and Metzudat David all paraphrase it as 'I am confident' or 'I know that you will answer'. The KJV 'wilt hear me' weakens 'answer' (ta'aneni, the word for a reply, not just for listening).

The vocabulary stacks the senses of hearing: 'incline your ear', 'hear'. To incline an ear is a physical image, a person leaning down toward a mouth, as a king leans from a high seat to the petitioner below. 'Utterance' (imrah) is a spoken word, a statement, not 'speech' in the KJV sense of an oration. 'El' is the generic word for God, not the divine name. Ibn Ezra says it is used here because God has the power to help; Radak's paraphrase is 'and you are able to help me' (Ibn Ezra, Radak on Psalm 17:6).

philological_notes.note: You will answer me. The root means to respond, not merely to listen; the KJV 'hear me' loses the reply. Rashi paraphrases 'I am confident that you will answer me'.
God, by the generic title rather than the name YHWH. Ibn Ezra says the title is chosen because God has power; Radak adds 'you are able to help me'.
Incline your ear: a bodily image, a listener bending toward the speaker.

verses.translation_literal: Make wonderful your loyal deeds, savior of those who take refuge, from those who rise up, by your right hand.
verses.translation_dramatic: Show me your faithful love, and make it a wonder. You save all who run to you for shelter. Save them from those who rise up against them, with your right hand.
verses.directors_commentary:
'Make wonderful' is the verb hafleh, from the root for wonder, and it carried both 'do something marvellous' and 'set apart'. Ibn Ezra, Radak and Metzudat Zion explain it as 'distinguish, separate', and Radak and Rashi cite Exodus 33:16 ('we shall be set apart, I and your people'). On that reading the speaker asks God to single out his covenant love for those who trust him. Meiri takes it as 'great publicity', a public wonder, and also records the 'separate' reading. The KJV 'Shew thy marvellous lovingkindness' takes only the 'wonder' sense.

'Lovingkindness' is Coverdale's coinage for chesed, the loyalty that bound partners in a covenant. 'Take refuge' (chasah) is a verb of shelter, not of 'trust': the people who run into the shadow of a stronger one. 'Those who rise up' is a participle, those in the act of rising, a word used of rebels and attackers. The 'right hand' is the strong hand. Whether 'by your right hand' modifies 'save' (KJV) or 'take refuge' (Ibn Ezra, who says the construction is not found without the preposition; others link it to 'savior') is open.

The commentators also divide on what 'rise up by your right hand' means. Radak reads the enemies as rebels against God's right hand, since everyone knows the kingship is David's from God, and whoever rebels against him rebels against God. Meiri records the same idea as one view. Malbim has them claim the opposite: that God's right hand is with them, as if God had sent them against David, and he asks God to show by a great kindness that the truth is not with them.

philological_notes.note: Make wonderful, or set apart. The Hiphil of the root for wonder; Ibn Ezra, Radak and Metzudat Zion take it as 'distinguish'.
Your acts of covenant loyalty (plural). KJV 'lovingkindness' is Coverdale's coinage.
Those who take refuge, shelter. The verb is about running to cover, not abstract trust.

Those who rise up, with 'by/against your right hand'. Radak: rebels against God's right hand, because rebelling against David is rebelling against God. Malbim: they claim that God's right hand is with them against David.

verses.translation_literal: Keep me like the pupil, daughter of an eye; in the shadow of your wings you will hide me.
verses.translation_dramatic: Guard me as you would guard the pupil of an eye, the very apple of it. Hide me in the shade of your wings.
verses.directors_commentary:
Two images, one of the body and one of the bird. The first is stranger in Hebrew than in English. 'Ishon' means 'little man': the pupil is so called because a tiny human figure is seen in it, and the ending -on makes it small (Radak, Meiri and Metzudat Zion on Psalm 17:8). Rashi derives the word differently, from the darkness of the pupil, as in 'in the pupil of darkness' (Prov 20:20), and adds that God set the eyelashes as its guard.

'Bat ayin', literally 'daughter of an eye', is not a second creature. Radak and Metzudat Zion say 'bat' is the name of the thing itself, the eyeball from which light comes, and 'ishon' is the descriptive name, so the two words are synonyms doubled, like 'dust of earth' in Daniel 12:2; Meiri likewise says 'ishon' that is 'bat ayin' are one. The KJV 'apple of the eye' is an old English idiom for the pupil (once thought to be a solid round object); it hides the little man, and the doubled name.

The eye is the most protected thing in the body, lid and lash and socket. The shadow of wings is an image the ancient world knew in stone: winged guardians over a throne or an ark. KJV 'under the shadow' is fine; but 'hide me' is the verb of concealment, not just shade. The Targum renders the second line 'in the shadow of your Shekhinah', where the Hebrew has wings.

philological_notes.note: 'Little man': the pupil, where a small image of a person is seen, with the diminutive ending -on. Rashi derives it instead from darkness (cf. Prov 20:20).
Literally 'daughter of an eye'; the name of the eyeball from which light comes. 'Ishon' and 'bat ayin' are synonyms placed together.
You will hide me: the verb of concealment, used of shelter from danger.

verses.translation_literal: From before wicked ones who have assailed me, my enemies who surround me with [lust for my] soul.
verses.translation_dramatic: Hide me from the wicked who have fallen on me, from the enemies who close around me, hungry for my very life.
verses.directors_commentary:
The danger is named at last. The word for 'wicked' (resha'im) is the legal opposite of the righteous of verse 1: the guilty party, not just a bad man. The verb shadad is the verb of plundering or assault, as of a raiding band; the KJV 'oppress' is too abstract, and the Hebrew names no goods or land, only the act. Ibn Ezra offers an alternative: shaduni is 'like' sevavuni, 'surrounded me'. The little word zu is a relative ('who'), as Ibn Ezra and Radak explain, and Radak cites Isaiah 42:24 (Ibn Ezra, Radak on Psalm 17:9).

The phrase 'be-nefesh' is hard: nefesh is the throat, the appetite, the life. KJV 'deadly enemies' is a guess at 'against my life'; YLT 'in soul' is literal. Radak and Metzudat David read 'to take my life'; Ibn Ezra reads 'with craving of the soul'; Meiri gives both and adds a third (Radak, Metzudat David, Ibn Ezra, Meiri on Psalm 17:9). The surrounding verb, 'they encircle', is the military language of siege. Notice the shift from the 'I' of the defense to the 'they' of the threat: this is the point where the courtroom becomes a battlefield.

philological_notes.note: They have assailed, plundered me: the verb of the raider, not simply 'oppress' (KJV). Ibn Ezra takes it as equivalent to 'surrounded me'.
With soul/life/appetite. Taken as 'to take my life' or 'with greedy desire'; the old commentaries differ.

verses.translation_literal: Their fat they have closed; their mouth they have spoken with pride.
verses.translation_dramatic: Fat has sealed their hearts shut, and out of those mouths comes nothing but pride.
verses.directors_commentary:
A sharp, bodily image of the enemy. In the ancient world fat was the sign of the rich and the secure, and a man grown fat on easy living was a man closed to the claims of others and to God. The Hebrew says simply 'their fat they have shut', and it does not say what is shut. Rashi hears the heart and the eyes shut to the fear of God; Radak and Metzudat David hear the mouth shut with fat, so that pride comes out as though from a stopped-up face; Malbim jokes that the fat itself speaks (Rashi, Radak, Metzudat David, Malbim on Psalm 17:10).

The KJV 'They are inclosed in their own fat' makes the verb a passive and makes the fat a prison, and neither is in the Hebrew: the verb is active ('they have closed') and the fat is its object. The ASV and Webster keep the KJV. The second line returns to the mouth, which links back to the 'lips of deceit' of verse 1: his mouth is truthful, theirs is proud. The word ge'ut, 'pride', is also 'swelling', the same rising as a river in flood.

philological_notes.note: Their fat. Fat as the sign of prosperity and of a dulled, insensitive heart (compare Ps 73:7; Deut 32:15).
Pride, loftiness; related to the rising of water or a swelling.

verses.translation_literal: Our steps, now, they have surrounded us; their eyes they set to turn [us] down on the ground.
verses.translation_dramatic: Now they have us ringed. Every step we take, they are there. Their eyes are fixed on us, watching for the moment to strike us to the ground.
verses.directors_commentary:
The speaker is suddenly 'we'. The tradition has a Ketiv/Qere here. Radak says the verb is written 'they have surrounded me' (Ketiv) and read 'us' (Qere), and explains the plural as David and the company that gathered to him when he fled Saul, the singular as himself, the chief of them; Meiri reports the assignment the other way round, written plural and read singular, and reads the same two voices into it (Radak, Meiri on Psalm 17:11). This translation follows the Qere, 'us'. The word 'now' marks a moment: the net has just closed.

The verse is full of foot and eye. 'Steps' (ashurim) is again the word for the footing of a walker; Radak and Meiri note the doubled shin and compare Job 31:7. The enemy sets his eyes on those steps and on the ground in front of them: the look of a hunter who reads the ground. The last clause is the most disputed: 'to turn, to bend' (linot) has no object. KJV 'bowing down to the earth' reads it as 'bowing them down', which Webster repeats; the YLT 'to turn aside in the land' keeps it blank; the ASV and BBE supply 'us'. Rashi explains 'to spread out on the ground', that is to strike down (Rashi on Psalm 17:11). Radak thinks they set a snare on the ground to catch us.

philological_notes.note: They have surrounded us (Qere). Radak says the written form (Ketiv) is 'me' and the read form 'us'; Meiri reports the opposite assignment. Both explain the plural/singular as David and his company.
To stretch out, bend down, turn aside. Without an object here; the sense must be supplied.

verses.translation_literal: His likeness [is] like a lion, [who] longs to tear, and like a young lion sitting in hiding places.
verses.translation_dramatic: He is a lion starving to tear. He is a young lion crouched in the dark of his lair.
verses.directors_commentary:
The plural enemies narrow to a single figure, 'his likeness', as a lion. In the ancient Near East the lion was the royal beast, the king's own symbol, and to say that an enemy is a lion is also to say that he is a king, or acts like one. Radak and Meiri identify him as Saul, with a parallel from Psalm 7:3 (Radak, Meiri on Psalm 17:12). Ibn Ezra reads 'his likeness' as true of each one of the circle.

Two lions in two lines: the 'aryeh' (full-grown lion) and the 'kefir' (young lion). The first 'longs to tear', the second 'sits in hiding places'. The KJV 'greedy of his prey' misreads the verb: kasaf is 'to long, yearn', the same verb as Laban's 'you longed, longed' for your father's house (Genesis 31:30), as Rashi notes (Rashi on Psalm 17:12). The lion in the text is not greedy but aching with hunger. And 'sitting' is a patient verb, a crouching waiting that is the opposite of a charge. KJV 'lurking' is fair, but 'secret places' is vague: mistarim are specific hiding holes, a thicket or a lair.

philological_notes.note: He longs, yearns. Not 'is greedy' (KJV). The verb of deep desire.
A young lion, one grown enough to hunt but still ambushing from cover, as Malbim notes.

verses.translation_literal: Arise, YHWH! Go before his face! Make him bow down! Deliver my life from the wicked, your sword.
verses.translation_dramatic: Rise, LORD. Rise now, and stand before his face, before the teeth close. Bring him down — let his knees fold under him. And pull my life out from the wicked man's grip: he is only your sword, and the sword is in your hand.
verses.directors_commentary:
Here the prayer turns from description to command, and the commands come in a rush of short imperatives: arise, confront, bring down, rescue. The speaker has just compared his enemies to a lion crouching in ambush (v. 12), and now asks God to do what a king's champion does, step out in front of the attacker. Say these lines like a man pushing a door that is about to give way.

The KJV 'disappoint him' is the great archaism of this verse. In 1611 'disappoint' still meant to unsettle or foil, but today it sounds like a letdown. The verb is קַדְּמָה, 'go ahead of', 'meet', 'forestall': meet him at the door before he reaches me. The next verb, הַכְרִיעֵהוּ, is the causative of כָּרַע, 'to kneel, to sink to the knees', the posture of a beaten soldier or a collapsing animal. So 'cast him down' is fair, but the image is of knees buckling, not of a throw. Then the KJV 'the wicked, which is thy sword' keeps the Hebrew apposition (the wicked man is God's sword), and that is a bold thought: even the oppressor is a weapon in God's hand, as Assyria is the rod of anger in Isaiah 10:5, which is how Radak reads it. Rashi and Malbim agree: God lets the wicked strike those who deserve it. Other translations (ASV, BBE) soften this to 'by your sword', which turns the oppressor into a bystander and God into the one who wields a separate weapon.

philological_notes.note: Piel imperative of קדם: go to meet, come before, forestall. It is the opposite of what the KJV's 'disappoint' sounds like to a modern ear. Here it is a request for God to get in front of the enemy before he arrives, as in Metzudat David's 'forestall him before he takes me'.
Hiphil of כרע, 'to bow, to sink to the knee': make him collapse onto his knees. Rashi explains it as striking the feet so that he kneels and falls.
'Your sword', in apposition to 'the wicked'. Whether the wicked man is God's instrument or the sword is the means of rescue is the main fork in the reading; the Hebrew has no preposition 'by'.

verses.translation_literal: From men, your hand, YHWH, from men, from the world, whose portion is in life, and your hidden store you fill their belly; their sons are sated, and they leave their abundance to their little ones.
verses.translation_dramatic: From men — men who are only your hand, LORD — from men whose whole world is this world, whose share is simply life, and nothing past it. You fill their bellies with what you had laid away. Their sons eat until they are full; and when they die, what is left over they hand down to the babies at their knees.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is the darkest knot in the psalm, and an actor should play it as bitter, tight and a little incredulous. The speaker has asked to be rescued from the wicked; now he describes someone, and he does it in a stammer: 'from men — your hand — from men — from the world.' The repetition is the sound of a man spitting out the word.

The verse has two main readings, and the translation layers follow the first. Ibn Ezra, Radak and Malbim take mittim as 'men' (the old plural of mat) and 'your hand' as naming them as God's instrument, as the wicked man was 'your sword' in verse 13 (Radak: 'as he called them your sword, he called them your hand'). 'Men of this world' (mi-cheled) are those whose whole desire is this world, whose portion is this life, and whom God fills with his stored-up good in this world only; Malbim adds that these are ordinary mortals who build and farm, as against the wicked who are God's sword (Ibn Ezra, Radak, Malbim on Psalm 17:14). Rashi, Metzudat David and the Targum hear it differently: 'from those who die by your hand', that is, 'on their beds I choose to be', and 'those who die in old age', whose portion in life is the life of the world to come, and whose belly God fills from the good he stored for those who fear him (Rashi on Ps 31:20, Metzudat David); the Targum has the righteous who give their lives for God's sake, whose portion is in the life of the world. Meiri reads it of David's tribe, Judah, kept under God's hand. Radak also reports the midrash that applies the verse to Rabbi Akiva and his companions, and the Holy One's answer 'their portion is in life' (Berakhot 61b). A director should decide which reading the actor is speaking.

The KJV 'which are thy hand' is faithful to the Hebrew, but 'men of the world, which have their portion in this life' makes the point sharper than the Hebrew does. 'In this life' is added; the text says only 'in life'. Then 'whose belly thou fillest with thy hid treasure' (KJV) follows the Qere, tzefunekha, 'what you have stored away'. The picture of the sated is plain in ancient terms: sons fed, an estate left, and wealth counted in children and inheritance. 'Their little ones' are olelim, toddlers, the youngest.

philological_notes.note: As pointed, 'from men', the old plural of mat 'man' (as in Deut 4:27, 'men of number'), with the next phrase naming them as God's hand. Rashi, Metzudat David and the Targum hear 'from those who die' (by God's hand, on their beds), and read the end of the verse as the world to come.

A poetic word for the passing world or the span of a lifetime, as in Ps 39:6 and 49:2. Metzudat Zion reads it as time; Ibn Ezra reads it as the world in which men are not lasting; Rashi derives it from 'rust' (the decay of old age).
Qere reading, 'what you have hidden, your store'. Radak: God fills their belly in this world with his stored goodness. Rashi: the good stored for those who fear God.
'Their little ones', young children; Metzudat Zion glosses 'their small sons'.

verses.translation_literal: I — in righteousness I will see your face; I will be sated, when awaking, with your likeness.
verses.translation_dramatic: But I — I will see your face, standing in righteousness. When I wake, I shall be full, and what fills me will be your likeness.
verses.directors_commentary:
After the heavy sentences of verse 14 the voice shifts: 'But I.' The very first word, ani, is a hinge, the speaker stepping away from the men with sated bellies. Their fullness is bread and sons; his will be a face. Note the echo: the wicked 'are sated' (yisbe'u), and he 'will be sated' (esbe'ah), the same verb, a different meal. Radak says it outright: they are sated in this world, and I in the world to come. Let the actor take one beat of silence before 'I' and then slow right down.

The KJV 'I will behold thy face in righteousness' is fair, and 'when I awake' is correct. 'Likeness' is the safe choice for temunah, a shape or form. Radak ties it to Numbers 12:8, 'he beholds the form (temunah) of the LORD': for him it is the grasp of the intellect of God's glory, according to the soul's power after it parts from the body. Moses had this in his bodily life, and that is what other prophets lack; the other prophets will have it after death. Radak adds that Ibn Ezra explains the verse of this world, as a vision of thought and not of the eye.

What 'awaking' means is the oldest question on the verse. Rashi reads it of the future and, as a second reading, of the waking of the dead from their sleep, when they are in the likeness of God's image (Gen 9:6); Metzudat David reads it as the resurrection (Dan 12:2). Radak reads it as the soul that does not die and sleep, against 'they shall sleep a perpetual sleep' (Jer 51:39). Ibn Ezra reads an ordinary waking, in clear thought and not in a dream. Meiri reads 'seeing the face' as a figure for the clinging of the intellect, 'without a screen or partition'. The Hebrew leaves it open.

philological_notes.note: 'I will see', a verb of visionary seeing, used of prophets and of gazing at a person of rank, not the everyday ראה.

Hiphil infinitive of יקץ, 'to wake up': 'in waking'. Whether it means a morning wake-up or waking from death is disputed: Rashi and Metzudat David read the waking of the dead, Radak the soul that does not sleep (Jer 51:39), Ibn Ezra an ordinary waking.
'Your form, your likeness'. Radak links it to Numbers 12:8, where Moses beholds the temunah of YHWH: an intellectual vision of God, which Moses had in life and others attain after death.
